# Market Selection — The Starving Crowd

**Source:** *$100M Offers*, "Pricing: Finding the Right Market — A Starving Crowd" (lines ~671–843).
Run this **before** building or pricing an offer. `hormozi-offer-market` uses it to pick/validate the
market and niche. "A Grand Slam Offer given to the wrong audience will fall on deaf ears" (l.661) — the
market is the box you check first.

The core reframe: **"We are not trying to *create* demand. We are trying to *channel* it"** (l.711). If
there's no market for the offer, nothing downstream works. Don't be romantic about your audience —
"serve the people who can pay you what you're worth" (l.709).

---

## The Starving Crowd principle

*Parable (l.677–685):* asked which single advantage he'd want for a hot-dog stand — location, quality,
price, taste — the professor answers **"A starving crowd."** With enough demand you "can be mediocre at
business, have a terrible offer, and have no ability to persuade people, and still make money" (l.687).
*Real pattern:* COVID toil-paper shortage — no offer, atrocious pricing, no pitch, yet rolls sold for
$100+ because the crowd was huge and starving (l.689).

*Cautionary pattern — Lloyd (l.691–703):* great product (one-click newspaper ad services), a zero-risk
revshare offer (he only got paid a % of revenue he added), natural sales skill — but the business
declined because **the market (newspapers) was shrinking ~25% every year.** Same entrepreneur pivoted
to automated mask manufacturing in COVID and hit **millions/month within 5 months** — same skill set, a
business he had zero experience in, different market. **Your market matters more than you do.**

---

## The three levers on success (in order)

```
   Starving Crowd (market)  >  Offer Strength  >  Persuasion Skills
```

Rate each **great / normal / bad** and move left→right in order of importance (l.759–765):
- A **"great"** on a higher-order lever **overpowers** everything lower.
- A **"normal"** passes the buck to the next lever.
- A **"bad"** **stops** the equation — *unless* a "great" from a higher lever nullifies it.

Worked examples (l.767–773):
- **Great market** beats a bad offer + bad persuasion (hot dogs to a 2am bar-close crowd — sell out).
- **Normal market + Grand Slam Offer (great)** = tons of money even with weak persuasion — *this is most
  readers, and the whole point of building a great offer.*
- **Normal market + normal offer** = you must be *exceptionally* good at persuasion (the hardest path).

**Practical floor:** you can't be in a **bad** (shrinking) market — nothing will work. A **normal**
market is fine; "there is a fortune to be made within normal markets" (l.761). Don't chase a "great"
market as a prerequisite — nail the offer instead.

---

## The four market indicators

A **"normal" market** = growing at ~the marketplace rate with common unmet needs in one of three
evergreen categories: **Health, Wealth, Relationships** (l.711, l.749) — these always exist because
lacking them is always painful. Evaluate any candidate market/niche against all four indicators:

### 1) Massive Pain
They must not merely *want* but **desperately need** the solution (l.719). "The degree of the pain is
proportional to the price you can charge" (l.721). **"The pain is the pitch"** (l.723) — articulate the
pain accurately and they almost always buy.
- **Evaluate:** How acute/frequent/expensive is the problem? Can you state their pain back to them
  precisely (so they "feel understood," l.729)? A prospect *must* have a painful problem for you to
  charge to solve.

### 2) Purchasing Power
The audience must be able to **afford** the price you need (l.737). *Anti-pattern:* a great résumé
service that couldn't get paid — the customers were all **unemployed** (l.733–735). Pain + volume +
easy targeting don't matter if they can't pay.
- **Evaluate:** Do targets have the money (or access to it) to pay your required price and make it worth
  your time?

### 3) Easy to Target
You must be able to **find and reach** them (l.739–743). Good signs: they belong to associations,
mailing lists, social-media groups, shared channels — "gathered together somewhere." Bad: needles in a
haystack.
- **Evaluate:** Is there a reachable, defined pool (list/group/channel) where your promotion lands on
  the right eyes? *(Wanting to serve, e.g., rich doctors is fine — they're findable; the point is your
  promotions must actually reach the intended audience, l.743.)*

### 4) Growing
Growing markets are a **tailwind**; declining markets a **headwind** (l.745). This is the one Lloyd
missed — newspapers had pain, purchasing power, and easy targeting, but were **shrinking fast** (l.747).
- **Evaluate:** Is the market at least holding, ideally growing? *Pattern:* "second-half-of-life"
  relationship coaching beats college-student relationships — seniors have more pain (nearer death),
  more buying power, are easy to find, **and** more people now turn 65 each year than turn 20 (growing)
  (l.753).

**Selection method (l.751–755):** start from what you're good at within Health / Wealth / Relationships,
then find a **smaller subgroup** inside it that scores strong on pain + money + targeting and **isn't
shrinking.**

---

## Commit to the niche

> **"Don't make me niche slap you"** (l.777).

Newer entrepreneurs try *one* offer in *one* market, don't get rich, wrongly conclude "bad market," and
**niche-hop** (dentists → chiropractors) — but both are normal markets worth billions; **either works,
just not both. Pick one. "No one can serve two masters"** (l.781). Every market has unpleasant traits —
the grass isn't greener; hopping forces you to restart the trial-and-error from zero each time (l.783).
**Pick, then commit long enough to fail your way to a Grand Slam Offer** (l.785, l.835). "If you try one
hundred offers, I promise you will succeed" (l.835). If an offer fails, "it doesn't mean you suck. It
means your offer sucks" (l.835).

### Riches are in the niches (why committing pays)
Niching down **makes far more money** — you can charge up to **100× more for essentially the same
product** (Dan Kennedy's lesson, l.807). *Worked pricing ladder (l.809–825):*
- Generic **"Time Management"** course → **$19** (nothing special).
- **"Time Management for Sales Professionals"** → **$99** (tie it to one more sale).
- **"Time Management for B2B Outbound Sales Reps"** → **$499** (their deals are big — 25× the generic).
- **"Time Management for B2B Outbound Power Tools & Gardening Sales Reps"** → **$1,000–$2,000** — "This
  is made exactly for me."
- Same core program throughout; specificity makes it more compelling *and* deliver more real value.
- Parallel pattern: generic weight-loss program ~$19 vs. one built only for shift-nurses ~$1,997 — same
  core ("eat less, move more"), ~100× the price (l.825).

**Specificity target:** be "the person who solves *this* problem for *this* type of person in *this*
unique way." *Gym Launch avatar pattern:* microgym owner, ~100 members, signed lease, ≥1 employee,
wants to help clients lose weight — and they **turned down** everyone else (no personal trainers, no
online coaches), because knowing exactly who it's for drove focus and high-converting messaging
(l.799–803).

---

## When to broaden (advice for most people)

- **Under $10M/year → niche DOWN; it makes more money** (l.795). Serving *fewer* clients *more narrowly*
  is almost always easier and more profitable at this stage.
- **$10M/year is already top ~0.4% (≈1 in 250 businesses)** — so **99.6% of readers should stay narrow**
  (l.795). Many companies reached **$30M+** on a single niche (chiropractors, gyms, plumbers, solar,
  roofers, salon owners) (l.797). "If you are at $1M or $3M thinking you've capped, you're wrong — you
  just need to be better" (l.797).
- **Above ~$10M, broadening depends on TAM** (total addressable market — a business can only grow to its
  TAM). When you genuinely need more room, broaden by going **up market, down market, or into an
  adjacent market** where your existing services still provide value (l.795).

**Decision rule:** default to committing and niching until you clearly outgrow the TAM; treat broadening
as a later, TAM-driven move — never as an escape from a hard offer.

---

## Output contract (for `hormozi-offer-market`)

Given the user's product, produce:
1. The **category** (Health / Wealth / Relationships) and the specific **niche/avatar** (as specific as
   the Gym Launch avatar — role + qualifiers, not "small business owners").
2. A **four-indicator scorecard** — Massive Pain, Purchasing Power, Easy to Target, Growing — each rated
   great/normal/bad with the evidence/reasoning, and an explicit **STOP** if the market is bad
   (shrinking) or lacks purchasing power.
3. The **three-lever read** (market > offer > persuasion) placing this market, so expectations are set.
4. A **commit recommendation** (the one niche to pick) and, if relevant, a **niche-pricing note** (how
   specificity supports a higher price) — with any price figures derived from the product or marked
   `<placeholder>`, never fabricated.
5. A **broaden/stay verdict** based on the ~$10M/TAM rule.
